title: Porous materials for sulfur dioxide capture from flue gas
content: Sulfur dioxide (SO2) emissions from fossil fuel combustion and industrial processes pose severe environmental and health risks, necessitating efficient flue gas desulfurization (FGD). Conventional FGD technologies are limited by high water consumption, secondary waste generation, and poor trace-level SO2 removal efficiency. Porous materials have emerged as promising adsorbents owing to their tunable pore structures, designable surface chemistry, mild operating conditions, and recyclability. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in porous materials for SO2 capture, with particular emphasis on the complementary roles of crystalline (zeolites, MOFs, COFs, HOFs, POCs, and MOCs) and amorphous (porous carbons, mesoporous oxides, POPs, ionic liquids, and related systems) adsorbents. Key adsorption mechanisms—including open metal sites, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, dipole–dipole interactions, acid–base interactions, alkaline functionalization, amine functionalization, modification with metals and alkaline components, metal oxide modification, nitrogen doping, loading of organic basic components, physisorption–chemisorption synergy, and catalytic oxidation—are critically discussed in the context of structure–performance relationships. Finally, current challenges and future perspectives are outlined to guide the development of high-performance, stable, regenerable, and industrially applicable SO2 adsorbents.
